title: Scheduling Arbitrary-Deadline Sporadic Task Systems on Multiprocessors

extraction.paper_name: Scheduling Arbitrary-Deadline Sporadic Task Systems on Multiprocessors
extraction.paper_description: This paper proposes EDF-SS(DTMIN/δ), a new task-splitting algorithm for scheduling arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems on multiprocessors. It can be used for both run-time scheduling and feasibility analysis. The algorithm is shown to offer improved schedulability compared to prior methods and provides a sufficient feasibility test with a processor speedup factor of (4 - 2/m).

formal_description.statement: A sporadic task tau_i is characterized by (C_i, T_i, D_i), where C_i is the worst-case execution time, T_i is the minimum inter-arrival time (period), and D_i is the relative deadline. We assume 0 <= C_i <= D_i and C_i <= T_i.

variables.C_i: Worst-case execution time of task i
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i

assumptions: Preemptive scheduling
Multiprocessor platform with m identical processors
Interprocessor migration permitted for split tasks
A job cannot execute on multiple processors simultaneously
Two jobs of the same task cannot execute simultaneously
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental parameters of a sporadic task in the system.

informal_sketch.intuition: This defines the basic properties of any task in our system: how much work it needs (C_i), how often it can arrive (T_i), and by when it must finish (D_i). These are standard real-time task parameters.
steps: Identify a task by its index 'i'.
Assign 'C_i' as the maximum CPU time it needs.
Assign 'T_i' as the minimum time between consecutive arrivals of jobs from this task.
Assign 'D_i' as the time limit from arrival by which a job must complete.
Ensure C_i is non-negative and less than or equal to D_i (execution cannot exceed deadline).
Ensure C_i is less than or equal to T_i (a task cannot demand more execution than its period, otherwise it's unschedulable on a uniprocessor).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Task:
    def __init__(self, id, C, T, D):
        self.id = id
        self.C = C
        self.T = T
        self.D = D
        # Assertions based on assumptions
        assert 0 <= C <= D, f"Task {id}: C ({C}) must be <= D ({D})"
        assert C <= T, f"Task {id}: C ({C}) must be <= T ({T})"
key_insights: These parameters are crucial for calculating workload and determining schedulability.
The C_i <= T_i constraint is fundamental for any task to be schedulable on a single processor, even if split.

formal_description.statement:
A task set is categorized based on its deadlines:
1. Implicit deadlines: for_all i : D_i = T_i
2. Constrained deadlines: for_all i : D_i <= T_i
3. Arbitrary deadlines: Otherwise (i.e., some D_i > T_i is allowed)

variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i

assumptions: Task Model Parameters are defined
formal_description.conclusion: Categorizes task systems based on the relationship between task deadlines and periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: This helps classify the complexity of scheduling. Implicit deadlines are the simplest, constrained are more complex, and arbitrary deadlines (where a task's deadline can be after its next arrival) are the most challenging.
steps: For each task tau_i in the task set:
Check if D_i == T_i for all tasks. If yes, it's an implicit deadline system.
Else, check if D_i <= T_i for all tasks. If yes, it's a constrained deadline system.
If neither of the above, then at least one task has D_i > T_i, making it an arbitrary deadline system.
key_insights: Arbitrary deadline systems are the most general and difficult to schedule because multiple jobs of the same task can be active simultaneously.

variables.DT_MIN: Minimum of all deadlines and periods in the task set
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i
variables.n: Total number of tasks in the system

assumptions: Task Model Parameters are defined
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a system-wide minimum time parameter used for slot sizing.

informal_sketch.intuition: DT_MIN represents the smallest time scale relevant to any task's timing constraints (either its deadline or its period). This value is used to determine the base slot size for the scheduling algorithm.
steps: Collect all D_i values for i from 1 to n.
Collect all T_i values for i from 1 to n.
Find the minimum value among all collected D_i and T_i values.
key_insights: DT_MIN provides a common, smallest time unit for the system, which is critical for synchronizing split task execution across processors.

formal_description.statement: S = DT_MIN / delta

variables.DT_MIN: Minimum of all deadlines and periods in the task set
variables.delta: An integer parameter (>= 1) selected by the designer

assumptions: DT_MIN is defined
delta is an integer >= 1
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fixed duration of time slots used for dispatching and managing split tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: The system divides time into fixed-size slots 'S'. This slot size is a tunable parameter, where a smaller 'S' (larger 'delta') allows for finer-grained control and potentially better schedulability but more preemptions.
steps: Obtain the calculated value of DT_MIN.
Choose an integer value for 'delta' (e.g., 1, 2, 4, or tending to infinity for feasibility analysis).
Divide DT_MIN by delta to get the slot duration S.
key_insights: The slot duration 'S' is a critical parameter that balances schedulability (smaller S is better) with preemption overhead (larger S is better).
Time slots are synchronized across all processors.

formal_description.statement: On processor p, x_p denotes the duration of the reserve at the beginning of a time slot for a split task shared with processor p-1. Analogously, z_p denotes the duration of the reserve at the final part of a time slot on processor p for a split task shared with processor p+1.

variables.x_p: Duration of the initial reserve on processor p
variables.z_p: Duration of the final reserve on processor p

assumptions: Time is subdivided into slots of duration S
Split tasks are assigned to two adjacent processors
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the dedicated time segments within each slot on a processor for executing split tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: To manage tasks split across two processors, each processor dedicates small, fixed-duration 'reserves' at the start and end of every time slot. These reserves are specifically for the split tasks, ensuring they get their allocated execution time.
steps: For each processor 'p' and each time slot:
Identify a duration 'x_p' at the beginning of the slot. This is for a task split between 'p-1' and 'p'.
Identify a duration 'z_p' at the end of the slot. This is for a task split between 'p' and 'p+1'.
key_insights: Reserves ensure that split tasks receive their allocated execution without interfering with non-split tasks' EDF scheduling.
The sum of x_p and z_p_minus_1 (for a task split between p-1 and p) determines the total reserve capacity for that split task.

formal_description.statement: tau_hi_p denotes the task that is split between processor p and processor p-1. Analogously, tau_lo_p denotes the task that is split between processor p and processor p+1.

variables.tau_hi_p: The split task that uses reserves x_p (on processor p) and z_p_minus_1 (on processor p-1)
variables.tau_lo_p: The split task that uses reserves z_p (on processor p) and x_p_plus_1 (on processor p+1)

assumptions: A task can be split between at most two processors
Processors are indexed p-1, p, p+1
formal_description.conclusion: Provides specific identifiers for the split tasks associated with a given processor's reserves.

informal_sketch.intuition: When a task is split, it runs partly on one processor and partly on an adjacent one. These identifiers help us refer to which specific split task is using the 'high' (p-1, p) or 'low' (p, p+1) side reserves of a processor 'p'.
steps: For a given processor 'p':
Identify the task, if any, that is split such that it uses processor 'p' and the processor immediately before it ('p-1'). Call this 'tau_hi_p'.
Identify the task, if any, that is split such that it uses processor 'p' and the processor immediately after it ('p+1'). Call this 'tau_lo_p'.
key_insights: This naming convention simplifies the calculation of execution demands for split tasks on a specific processor.

formal_description.statement: slot_exec(t, r) = floor(t / S) * r + min(t - floor(t / S) * S, r)

variables.slot_exec: Function to calculate execution in reserves
variables.r: Duration of a single reserve (e.g., x_p or z_p)

assumptions: S is defined
Reserves 'r' occur once per slot 'S'
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the amount of execution performed by a split task in a time interval 't', assuming it executes in all its reserves of duration 'r'.

informal_sketch.intuition: This function estimates how much total time a split task can execute within a given interval 't', assuming it always gets its dedicated reserve 'r' within each slot 'S'. It accounts for full slots and any partial slot at the end of the interval.
steps: Calculate the number of full time slots that fit into the interval 't': `num_full_slots = floor(t / S)`.
Multiply `num_full_slots` by the reserve duration 'r' to get execution from full slots.
Calculate the remaining time in the interval after full slots: `remaining_time = t - num_full_slots * S`.
The execution in this `remaining_time` is limited by either `remaining_time` itself or the reserve duration 'r', whichever is smaller.
Sum the execution from full slots and the remaining time to get `slot_exec(t, r)`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def slot_exec(t, r, S):
    num_full_slots = math.floor(t / S)
    execution_from_full_slots = num_full_slots * r
    remaining_time = t - num_full_slots * S
    execution_from_partial_slot = min(remaining_time, r)
    return execution_from_full_slots + execution_from_partial_slot
key_insights: This function is a building block for calculating the total demand of split tasks over arbitrary intervals.
It assumes optimal utilization of reserves within the given interval.

formal_description.statement: dbf(tau_set, L) = sum_{tau_j in tau_set} max(0, floor((L - D_j) / T_j) + 1) * C_j

variables.T_j: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task j
variables.C_j: Worst-case execution time of task j

assumptions: Task Model Parameters are defined
Jobs arrive no earlier than the beginning of L and have deadlines no later than the end of L
formal_description.conclusion: Represents the maximum cumulative execution requirement of a set of tasks within any time interval of duration L, assuming jobs arrive and have deadlines within that interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: The demand bound function (dbf) tells us the maximum amount of CPU time a task (or set of tasks) *needs* to execute within a given interval 'L' to meet its deadlines. It counts how many jobs of each task could arrive and have their deadlines fall within or by the end of 'L'.
steps: Initialize total demand `demand = 0`.
For each task `tau_j` in `tau_set`:
Calculate the number of jobs of `tau_j` that could arrive and have deadlines within `L`: `num_jobs = floor((L - D_j) / T_j) + 1`.
Ensure `num_jobs` is not negative (if `L < D_j`, no job can arrive and complete within `L`): `num_jobs = max(0, num_jobs)`.
Add the execution requirement of these jobs to the total demand: `demand += num_jobs * C_j`.
Return the `demand`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def dbf(task_set, L):
    total_demand = 0
    for task_j in task_set:
        # Number of jobs whose arrival is at or after 0 and deadline is at or before L
        # This formula is for jobs that *must* complete by L
        num_jobs = math.floor((L - task_j.D) / task_j.T) + 1
        num_jobs = max(0, num_jobs)
        total_demand += num_jobs * task_j.C
    return total_demand
key_insights: dbf is a fundamental tool for uniprocessor schedulability analysis, especially for EDF.
It provides a worst-case workload estimate for a given interval length.

formal_description.statement: active_slots(t, p) = floor(t / T_hi_p) * (min(D_hi_p, T_hi_p) / S) + floor(t / T_lo_p) * (min(D_lo_p, T_lo_p) / S)

variables.active_slots: Maximum number of effective slots for split tasks

assumptions: tau_hi_p and tau_lo_p are defined
S is defined
formal_description.conclusion: Calculates an upper bound on the number of 'active' time slots (where split tasks might execute) for the split tasks associated with processor p within a time interval t.

informal_sketch.intuition: This function estimates how many 'effective' slots (multiples of S) are needed by the split tasks on processor 'p' within an interval 't'. It considers how many jobs of each split task (tau_hi_p and tau_lo_p) could arrive in 't' and for each job, how many slots it might occupy based on its effective deadline.
steps: For `tau_hi_p`:
Calculate the number of jobs of `tau_hi_p` that could arrive in interval `t`: `num_jobs_hi = floor(t / T_hi_p)`.
Calculate the number of slots required per job of `tau_hi_p`: `slots_per_job_hi = min(D_hi_p, T_hi_p) / S`.
Total slots for `tau_hi_p`: `num_jobs_hi * slots_per_job_hi`.
Repeat similar calculations for `tau_lo_p`.
Sum the total slots for `tau_hi_p` and `tau_lo_p`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def active_slots(t, p, S, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p):
    slots_hi = 0
    if tau_hi_p:
        num_jobs_hi = math.floor(t / tau_hi_p.T)
        slots_per_job_hi = math.ceil(min(tau_hi_p.D, tau_hi_p.T) / S) # Note: paper uses /S, but for integer slots, it should be ceil or floor depending on context. Assuming integer slots for simplicity.
        slots_hi = num_jobs_hi * slots_per_job_hi

    slots_lo = 0
    if tau_lo_p:
        num_jobs_lo = math.floor(t / tau_lo_p.T)
        slots_per_job_lo = math.ceil(min(tau_lo_p.D, tau_lo_p.T) / S)
        slots_lo = num_jobs_lo * slots_per_job_lo

    return slots_hi + slots_lo
key_insights: This function helps quantify the potential for preemption events related to split tasks by estimating how many slot boundaries might be 'active' for them.
The `min(D_i, T_i) / S` term reflects the effective duration a split task job needs to complete, expressed in slots.

formal_description.statement: jobs(t, p) denotes the maximum number of jobs that are released during a time interval of duration t from either (i) non-split tasks assigned to processor p or (ii) the task split between processor p-1 and p (tau_hi_p) or (iii) the task split between processor p+1 and p (tau_lo_p).

variables.tau_P: Set of non-split tasks assigned to processor p
variables.tau_hi_p: Split task between p-1 and p
variables.tau_lo_p: Split task between p and p+1

assumptions: Task Model Parameters are defined
tau_hi_p and tau_lo_p are defined
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the total number of job arrivals relevant to processor p within a given interval t, which can trigger preemptions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This counts the maximum number of times a new job could arrive on processor 'p' within an interval 't'. Each new job arrival is a potential preemption point, so this helps bound preemption frequency.
steps: Initialize `total_job_arrivals = 0`.
For each non-split task `tau_j` in `tau_P` (tasks fully assigned to processor p):
Calculate `num_jobs_j = floor(t / T_j) + 1` (worst-case arrivals in interval t).
Add `num_jobs_j` to `total_job_arrivals`.
If `tau_hi_p` exists:
Calculate `num_jobs_hi = floor(t / T_hi_p) + 1`.
Add `num_jobs_hi` to `total_job_arrivals`.
If `tau_lo_p` exists:
Calculate `num_jobs_lo = floor(t / T_lo_p) + 1`.
Add `num_jobs_lo` to `total_job_arrivals`.
Return `total_job_arrivals`.
key_insights: Job arrivals are one of the primary causes of preemptions in dynamic priority scheduling like EDF.
This definition aggregates all potential job arrivals that could affect processor 'p'.

formal_description.statement: A feasibility test is said to have a processor speedup factor s if any task system deemed to not be feasible upon a particular platform by the test is guaranteed to actually not be feasible upon a platform in which each processor is 1/s times as fast.

variables.feasibility_test: An algorithm to determine if a task system is feasible

assumptions: A task system is feasible if all jobs meet deadlines on a given platform
formal_description.conclusion: Quantifies the 'optimality' or 'tightness' of a feasibility test. A smaller 's' means the test is closer to being exact (s=1 for an exact test, s=infinity for a test that performs arbitrarily poorly).

informal_sketch.intuition: The speedup factor tells you how much faster your processors would need to be for a task set, rejected by a test, to *actually* be unschedulable. If a test says a system isn't feasible on current processors, but it *would* be feasible if the processors were only slightly faster (e.g., 1.2x faster), then the test has a speedup factor of 1.2. A perfect test has a speedup factor of 1.
steps: Consider a task system and a platform (m processors of a certain speed).
Apply a feasibility test. If the test says the system is NOT feasible on this platform.

Then, if the actual optimal scheduler *also* cannot schedule the system on a platform where each processor is `1/s` times as fast (i.e., `s` times slower than the original platform), then 's' is the speedup factor.
Equivalently, if a system *is* feasible on a platform with processors of speed `X`, the test might only guarantee it's schedulable on processors of speed `s*X`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def evaluate_speedup_factor(feasibility_test, optimal_scheduler):
    # This is a conceptual evaluation, not a direct computation
    # s = 1 means the test is exact (if test says no, optimal says no on same speed)
    # s > 1 means the test is pessimistic (if test says no, optimal might say yes on slightly slower processors)
    pass
key_insights: A lower speedup factor indicates a better (less pessimistic) sufficient feasibility test.
It provides a quantitative performance guarantee for sufficient tests.

formal_description.statement: For any job J_i_k of a split task tau_i, it is required that J_i_k completes C_i time units within min(D_i, T_i) / S * S time units after its arrival.

variables.C_i: Worst-case execution time of task i
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i

assumptions: Task Model Parameters are defined
Slot Duration S is defined
This is a design choice for split tasks to ensure deadlines and prevent self-overlap.
formal_description.conclusion: Establishes a stricter, slot-aligned effective deadline for split tasks to simplify analysis and guarantee completion before the next job's arrival.

informal_sketch.intuition: For split tasks, we don't just aim for the original deadline D_i. We impose a tighter, slot-aligned deadline, `min(D_i, T_i) / S * S`. This ensures that a split task job finishes not only by its deadline but also before its next job could arrive, preventing complex scenarios where two jobs of the same split task are active simultaneously.
steps: Calculate `min(D_i, T_i)` for the split task `tau_i`.
Divide this by the slot duration `S` and take the floor (implicitly, as `min(D_i, T_i) / S` is used as a multiplier).
Multiply by `S` again to get a duration that is an integer multiple of `S`.
This calculated duration is the maximum time allowed for `J_i_k` to complete its `C_i` execution.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def get_split_task_effective_deadline(task_i, S):
    # The paper implies floor(min(D_i, T_i) / S) * S for the duration
    # The formula is min(D_i, T_i) / S * S, which implies min(D_i, T_i) is a multiple of S or floor is implicit.
    # Assuming the intent is to align to slot boundaries:
    effective_duration = math.floor(min(task_i.D, task_i.T) / S) * S
    return effective_duration

# Schedulability check for a split job J_i_k:
# if actual_completion_time(J_i_k) <= arrival_time(J_i_k) + get_split_task_effective_deadline(tau_i, S): 
#    J_i_k meets its deadline.
key_insights: This stricter deadline simplifies the analysis of split tasks by ensuring they complete within a predictable, slot-aligned window.
The `min(D_i, T_i)` part ensures that the job finishes before its next potential arrival, avoiding self-interference.

results.identifier: Claim: Reserve Dimensioning for Split Tasks

formal_description.statement: For a split task tau_i shared between processor p-1 and p, the reserves x_p and z_p_minus_1 are chosen such that x_p + z_p_minus_1 = C_i / (min(D_i, T_i) / S).

variables.x_p: Initial reserve duration on processor p
variables.z_p_minus_1: Final reserve duration on processor p-1
variables.C_i: Worst-case execution time of task i
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i

assumptions: Claim: Split Task Effective Deadline is met
The total execution available for tau_i in its effective deadline window is min(D_i, T_i) / S * (x_p + z_p_minus_1)
formal_description.conclusion: Defines how the durations of the reserves for a split task are set to exactly match its execution requirement within its effective deadline window.

informal_sketch.intuition: This formula ensures that the total 'reserve capacity' allocated to a split task across its two processors is exactly enough to meet its execution requirement (C_i) within its effective deadline. It's like saying, 'if you need 10 units of work done in 5 slots, each slot must provide 2 units of reserve'.
steps: Identify the split task `tau_i` and the two processors it uses (e.g., `p-1` and `p`).
Determine the total reserve duration needed per slot for `tau_i`: `reserve_per_slot = C_i / (min(D_i, T_i) / S)`.
This `reserve_per_slot` is then distributed between `x_p` (on processor `p`) and `z_p_minus_1` (on processor `p-1`) such that their sum equals `reserve_per_slot`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def dimension_split_task_reserves(task_i, S):
    # Calculate the total number of slots available for task_i within its effective deadline
    num_effective_slots = math.floor(min(task_i.D, task_i.T) / S)
    if num_effective_slots == 0:
        # Handle case where effective deadline is less than S, which might imply unschedulability or special handling
        return 0, 0 # Or raise error

    # Calculate the required total reserve duration per slot for task_i
    required_reserve_per_slot = task_i.C / num_effective_slots

    # This required_reserve_per_slot is then split between x_p and z_p_minus_1
    # The paper doesn't specify the split ratio, only the sum.
    # For example, it could be split equally:
    x_p = required_reserve_per_slot / 2
    z_p_minus_1 = required_reserve_per_slot / 2
    return x_p, z_p_minus_1
key_insights: This formula directly links a split task's execution requirement (C_i) to the physical reserve durations (x_p, z_p_minus_1) on the processors.
It ensures that the 'inflation' (reserves exceeding execution) is minimized for delta < infinity, and zero for delta -> infinity.

results.identifier: Claim: Execution Distribution for Split Tasks

formal_description.statement: If a job released by a split task tau_i executes for C_i time units, then it executes exactly (min(D_i, T_i) / S) * x_p time units on processor p and (min(D_i, T_i) / S) * z_p_minus_1 time units on processor p-1.

variables.C_i: Worst-case execution time of task i
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i
variables.x_p: Initial reserve duration on processor p
variables.z_p_minus_1: Final reserve duration on processor p-1

assumptions: Claim: Reserve Dimensioning for Split Tasks is applied
The job fully utilizes its allocated reserves
formal_description.conclusion: Specifies the exact distribution of a split task's total execution time across the two processors it is assigned to, based on the dimensioned reserves.

informal_sketch.intuition: Once we've decided how much total reserve time a split task gets per slot (x_p + z_p_minus_1), this claim states that the total execution on each processor is simply the per-slot reserve multiplied by the number of effective slots. It's a direct consequence of how reserves are dimensioned.
steps: Calculate the number of effective slots available for `tau_i`: `num_effective_slots = min(D_i, T_i) / S`.
Multiply `num_effective_slots` by `x_p` to get the total execution on processor `p`.
Multiply `num_effective_slots` by `z_p_minus_1` to get the total execution on processor `p-1`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_split_task_execution_distribution(task_i, S, x_p, z_p_minus_1):
    num_effective_slots = math.floor(min(task_i.D, task_i.T) / S)
    execution_on_p = num_effective_slots * x_p
    execution_on_p_minus_1 = num_effective_slots * z_p_minus_1
    return execution_on_p, execution_on_p_minus_1

# Assert that execution_on_p + execution_on_p_minus_1 == task_i.C if reserves are perfectly dimensioned.
key_insights: This property is crucial for accurately accounting for the workload contributed by split tasks to each individual processor.
It confirms that the C_i execution is precisely distributed according to the reserve allocations.

dependencies: Claim: Reserve Dimensioning for Split Tasks

results.identifier: Lemma: Upper Bound on Single Split Task Execution (Formula 7)

formal_description.statement:
The amount of execution of task tau_hi_p on processor p during a time interval of duration L is at most:
floor((L + S - x_p) / T_hi_p) * C_hi_p * (x_p / (x_p + z_p_minus_1)) + slot_exec(min(L + S - x_p - floor((L + S - x_p) / T_hi_p) * T_hi_p, min(D_hi_p, T_hi_p) / S * S), x_p)

variables.tau_hi_p: Split task between processor p and p-1
variables.x_p: Initial reserve duration on processor p for tau_hi_p
variables.z_p_minus_1: Final reserve duration on processor p-1 for tau_hi_p
variables.slot_exec: Function to calculate execution in reserves

assumptions: Task Model Parameters are defined
Slot Duration S is defined
Reserves x_p, z_p_minus_1 are defined and dimensioned
Split Task Identifiers (tau_hi_p) are defined
slot_exec function is defined
All jobs from split tasks execute for their maximum execution time C_hi_p
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a worst-case upper bound on the execution time that a specific split task (tau_hi_p) can demand on processor p within any interval of length L.

informal_sketch.intuition: This complex formula calculates the maximum execution time for one specific split task (tau_hi_p) on processor 'p' over an interval 'L'. It accounts for jobs that arrive just before 'L' and extend into it, and for jobs that arrive within 'L'. It uses the `slot_exec` function to handle the reserve-based execution within slots.
steps: **Part 1: Full jobs contribution.** Calculate how many full jobs of `tau_hi_p` could potentially contribute to execution on processor `p` within an extended interval `L + S - x_p` (to account for jobs arriving just before `L`). For each such job, it contributes `C_hi_p * (x_p / (x_p + z_p_minus_1))` execution to processor `p` (this is the fraction of its total execution C_hi_p that occurs on processor p, based on reserve dimensioning).

**Part 2: Partial job/remaining interval contribution.** Calculate the execution from any partial job or the remaining part of the interval `L + S - x_p` after accounting for full jobs. This remaining duration is then passed to `slot_exec` along with `x_p` (the reserve duration on processor `p`) to determine the maximum execution from reserves in that partial period. The `min(D_hi_p, T_hi_p) / S * S` term ensures this partial execution doesn't exceed the task's effective deadline duration.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_tau_hi_p_execution_bound(L, S, x_p, z_p_minus_1, tau_hi_p, slot_exec_func):
    if not tau_hi_p: return 0

    # Part 1: Contribution from full jobs
    # Extended interval to consider arrivals that might start before L but execute in L
    extended_L_for_arrivals = L + S - x_p
    num_full_jobs = math.floor(extended_L_for_arrivals / tau_hi_p.T)
    
    # Fraction of C_hi_p that executes on processor p
    if (x_p + z_p_minus_1) == 0: # Avoid division by zero if no reserves are allocated
        fraction_on_p = 0
    else:
        fraction_on_p = x_p / (x_p + z_p_minus_1)
    
    execution_from_full_jobs = num_full_jobs * tau_hi_p.C * fraction_on_p

    # Part 2: Contribution from partial job / remaining interval
    remaining_time_after_full_jobs = extended_L_for_arrivals - num_full_jobs * tau_hi_p.T
    
    # Effective deadline duration for split task
    effective_deadline_duration = math.floor(min(tau_hi_p.D, tau_hi_p.T) / S) * S

    # The min() here ensures we don't count execution beyond the task's effective deadline
    slot_exec_interval = min(remaining_time_after_full_jobs, effective_deadline_duration)
    execution_from_partial_slots = slot_exec_func(slot_exec_interval, x_p, S)

    return execution_from_full_jobs + execution_from_partial_slots
key_insights: This lemma is crucial for accurately modeling the demand of split tasks on a processor, which is more complex than non-split tasks due to their distributed execution.
It accounts for the 'carry-in' effect where a job might start before the interval L but still execute within it.
The use of `slot_exec` correctly models the discrete, slot-based execution of split tasks.

formal_description.statement:
The amount of execution of split tasks on processor p during a time interval of duration L is at most:
floor((L + S - x_p) / T_hi_p) * C_hi_p * (x_p / (x_p + z_p_minus_1)) + slot_exec(min(L + S - x_p - floor((L + S - x_p) / T_hi_p) * T_hi_p, min(D_hi_p, T_hi_p) / S * S), x_p) +
floor((L + S - z_p) / T_lo_p) * C_lo_p * (z_p / (x_p_plus_1 + z_p)) + slot_exec(min(L + S - z_p - floor((L + S - z_p) / T_lo_p) * T_lo_p, min(D_lo_p, T_lo_p) / S * S), z_p)

variables.x_p: Initial reserve duration on processor p for tau_hi_p
variables.z_p_minus_1: Final reserve duration on processor p-1 for tau_hi_p
variables.x_p_plus_1: Initial reserve duration on processor p+1 for tau_lo_p
variables.z_p: Final reserve duration on processor p for tau_lo_p
variables.tau_hi_p: Split task between processor p and p-1
variables.tau_lo_p: Split task between processor p and p+1

assumptions: Lemma: Upper Bound on Single Split Task Execution (Formula 7) is valid
A processor can host at most two split tasks (one tau_hi_p, one tau_lo_p)
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a worst-case upper bound on the total execution time that all split tasks assigned to processor p can demand within any interval of length L.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma combines the execution bounds for the two possible split tasks (tau_hi_p and tau_lo_p) that might execute on a given processor 'p'. It's simply the sum of the individual execution bounds derived in the previous lemma, applied to both the 'high' and 'low' split tasks.
steps: Calculate the execution bound for `tau_hi_p` on processor `p` using the formula from Lemma 2.4.1 (Formula 7).
Calculate the execution bound for `tau_lo_p` on processor `p` using an analogous formula (swapping `x_p` with `z_p`, `p-1` with `p+1`, and `hi` with `lo`).
Sum these two bounds to get the total execution of split tasks on processor `p`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_total_split_task_execution_bound(L, S, x_p, z_p_minus_1, x_p_plus_1, z_p, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p, slot_exec_func):
    # Calculate execution for tau_hi_p (split with p-1)
    exec_hi = 0
    if tau_hi_p:
        extended_L_hi = L + S - x_p
        num_full_jobs_hi = math.floor(extended_L_hi / tau_hi_p.T)
        fraction_on_p_hi = x_p / (x_p + z_p_minus_1) if (x_p + z_p_minus_1) > 0 else 0
        exec_hi_full = num_full_jobs_hi * tau_hi_p.C * fraction_on_p_hi
        remaining_time_hi = extended_L_hi - num_full_jobs_hi * tau_hi_p.T
        effective_deadline_hi = math.floor(min(tau_hi_p.D, tau_hi_p.T) / S) * S
        exec_hi_partial = slot_exec_func(min(remaining_time_hi, effective_deadline_hi), x_p, S)
        exec_hi = exec_hi_full + exec_hi_partial

    # Calculate execution for tau_lo_p (split with p+1)
    exec_lo = 0
    if tau_lo_p:
        extended_L_lo = L + S - z_p
        num_full_jobs_lo = math.floor(extended_L_lo / tau_lo_p.T)
        fraction_on_p_lo = z_p / (x_p_plus_1 + z_p) if (x_p_plus_1 + z_p) > 0 else 0
        exec_lo_full = num_full_jobs_lo * tau_lo_p.C * fraction_on_p_lo
        remaining_time_lo = extended_L_lo - num_full_jobs_lo * tau_lo_p.T
        effective_deadline_lo = math.floor(min(tau_lo_p.D, tau_lo_p.T) / S) * S
        exec_lo_partial = slot_exec_func(min(remaining_time_lo, effective_deadline_lo), z_p, S)
        exec_lo = exec_lo_full + exec_lo_partial

    return exec_hi + exec_lo
key_insights: This lemma provides the complete demand model for split tasks on a single processor, which is essential for the overall schedulability test.
It aggregates the worst-case demands from all split tasks that might contend for resources on processor 'p'.

Split tasks are scheduled in their dedicated reserves

Techniques from [9] for identifying testing sets are applicable
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a sufficient schedulability test for a single processor 'p' considering both its fully assigned (non-split) tasks and the portions of split tasks it hosts.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the core schedulability test for each individual processor. It states that if the total demand for execution on a processor (from both its dedicated tasks and its share of split tasks) never exceeds the available time 'L' for any interval 'L', then all tasks on that processor will meet their deadlines. This extends the uniprocessor EDF schedulability test to account for split tasks.
steps: For a given processor `p`:
Identify `tau_P`, the set of non-split tasks assigned entirely to `p`.
For any interval length `L`:
Calculate the demand from `tau_P` using `dbf(tau_P, L)`.
Calculate the demand from split tasks on `p` using `split_task_execution_bound_L` (Formula 8).
Sum these two demands to get `f(L)`.
Check if `f(L) <= L`. If this holds for all relevant `L > 0`, then processor `p` is schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def check_processor_schedulability(processor_p, L_values, S, x_p, z_p_minus_1, x_p_plus_1, z_p, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p):
    tau_P = processor_p.non_split_tasks
    for L in L_values: # L_values are the critical testing points
        demand_non_split = dbf(tau_P, L)
        demand_split = calculate_total_split_task_execution_bound(L, S, x_p, z_p_minus_1, x_p_plus_1, z_p, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p, slot_exec)
        f_L = demand_non_split + demand_split
        if f_L > L:
            return False # Processor p is not schedulable
    return True # Processor p is schedulable
key_insights: This theorem adapts the well-known uniprocessor EDF schedulability test to the task-splitting paradigm.
It combines the demand of traditional tasks with the carefully derived demand of split tasks.
The condition needs to be checked only for a finite (though potentially large) set of L values.

formal_description.statement:
Let n_preempt(t, p) denote an upper bound on the number of preemptions generated on processor p in a time interval of duration t. We then have that:
n_preempt(t, p) = jobs(t, p) + 2 + 3 * min(floor(t / S), active_slots(t, p))

variables.n_preempt: Upper bound on number of preemptions
variables.jobs: Maximum number of job arrivals (Definition: jobs(t, p))
variables.active_slots: Maximum number of effective slots for split tasks (Definition: active_slots(t, p))

assumptions: Preemptions occur only when a job arrives or a reserve begins/ends
jobs(t, p) is defined
active_slots(t, p) is defined
Slot Duration S is defined
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the total number of preemptions that can occur on a processor within a given time interval, considering both job arrivals and slot boundary events.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem quantifies the preemption overhead. Preemptions happen when new jobs arrive (handled by `jobs(t, p)`) or when the scheduler switches between split tasks and non-split tasks at slot boundaries. The `3 * min(floor(t / S), active_slots(t, p))` term accounts for these slot-related preemptions.
steps: Calculate `jobs(t, p)`: the maximum number of job arrivals (non-split and split tasks) in interval `t`.
Calculate `floor(t / S)`: the number of full time slots in interval `t`.
Calculate `active_slots(t, p)`: the maximum number of effective slots where split tasks might execute.

The number of slot-related preemption points is `min(floor(t / S), active_slots(t, p))`. Each such point can cause up to 3 preemptions (start of x_p, end of x_p/start of non-split, start of z_p/end of non-split, end of z_p). The proof states 'at most three preemptions caused by the beginning or ending of reserves' per slot.
Add 2 for the beginning and ending of the interval `L` itself.
Sum these components to get `n_preempt(t, p)`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_preemption_bound(t, p, S, jobs_func, active_slots_func, tau_P, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p):
    num_job_arrivals = jobs_func(t, p, tau_P, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p)
    
    # Number of full slots in interval t
    num_full_slots = math.floor(t / S)
    
    # Number of active slots for split tasks
    num_active_slots = active_slots_func(t, p, S, tau_hi_p, tau_lo_p)
    
    # Preemptions due to slot boundaries
    slot_boundary_preemptions = 3 * min(num_full_slots, num_active_slots)
    
    # Add 2 for the start and end of the interval t itself
    total_preemptions = num_job_arrivals + 2 + slot_boundary_preemptions
    return total_preemptions
key_insights: This theorem provides a quantitative measure of the run-time overhead, which is important for practical implementation.
It highlights the trade-off: smaller `S` (larger `delta`) leads to more preemptions but potentially better schedulability.
The bound is derived by considering discrete events: job arrivals and slot boundary transitions.

formal_description.statement: If an arbitrary sporadic task system is feasible on m identical processors each of a particular computing capacity, then the scheduling algorithm in [7] successfully partitions this system upon a platform comprised of m processors that are each (4 - 2/m) times as fast.
assumptions: Definition 1: Processor Speedup Factor is understood
The scheduling algorithm in [7] is a partitioning algorithm for arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems.
formal_description.conclusion: The partitioning algorithm from [7] has a processor speedup factor of (4 - 2/m).

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem, borrowed from prior work, gives a performance guarantee for a specific partitioning algorithm. It says that if a task system *could* be scheduled by an optimal algorithm on 'm' processors of a certain speed, then the algorithm from [7] can schedule it if those 'm' processors are (4 - 2/m) times faster. This means the algorithm from [7] is pessimistic by a factor of (4 - 2/m).
steps: Assume an arbitrary sporadic task system is feasible on 'm' processors with speed 'X' (by an optimal scheduler).
The algorithm from [7] is guaranteed to successfully partition and schedule this system if the processors are of speed `(4 - 2/m) * X`.
Therefore, the speedup factor for the algorithm in [7] is `(4 - 2/m)`.
key_insights: This theorem establishes a baseline quantitative performance guarantee for a state-of-the-art partitioning algorithm for arbitrary-deadline systems.
It's used as a benchmark against which the new FEAS-SS algorithm is compared.

formal_description.statement: The feasibility test FEAS-SS has a processor speedup factor <= (4 - 2/m) upon m-processor platforms.
assumptions: Definition 1: Processor Speedup Factor is understood
Theorem 2 (From [7]) is valid
FEAS-SS strictly dominates the partitioning algorithm of [7] (i.e., if [7] deems a system schedulable, FEAS-SS also deems it schedulable).
formal_description.conclusion: FEAS-SS provides a quantitative performance guarantee that is at least as good as the prior algorithm from [7].

informal_sketch.intuition: Since FEAS-SS can schedule every task system that the algorithm from [7] can schedule (and more), its performance guarantee (speedup factor) must be at least as good as, or better than, that of the algorithm from [7]. Therefore, its speedup factor is bounded by the same value.
steps: Recall Theorem 2: The algorithm from [7] has a speedup factor of `(4 - 2/m)`.
FEAS-SS is designed to 'dominate' the algorithm from [7], meaning any system schedulable by [7] is also schedulable by FEAS-SS.
If FEAS-SS can schedule *at least as many* systems as [7], then its speedup factor cannot be worse than [7]'s.
Thus, `s_FEAS_SS <= (4 - 2/m)`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def speedup_factor_FEAS_SS(m):
    # Since FEAS-SS dominates the algorithm from [7],
    # its speedup factor is at least as good.
    return 4 - (2 / m)

key_insights: This theorem provides a strong theoretical guarantee for FEAS-SS, showing it's not only empirically better but also theoretically bounded.
The dominance property is key to inheriting the speedup factor from the prior work.
